Under the U.S. Constitution (Article I, Section 7), once a bill passes both houses of Congress it must be presented to the President for approval or veto [d1]. The President has 10 days to sign or veto the enrolled bill; if signed, it becomes law, and if vetoed, it is returned to Congress with objections [d3][d7]. The Framers gave the President this veto power specifically to prevent the legislative branch from becoming too powerful, as part of the system of checks and balances [d4][d10]. Congress, however, retains the authority to override a presidential veto by a two-thirds majority vote of both the House and Senate [d5][d6][d7]. A special case is the "pocket veto": if the President does not sign or return a bill and Congress adjourns before the 10-day period expires, the bill does not become law and this pocket veto cannot be overridden by Congress [d2][d6][d8]. Conversely, if Congress remains in session and the President neither signs nor vetoes within 10 days (excluding Sundays), the bill automatically becomes law [d6][d7].
